stem: A 68-year-old patient newly diagnosed with heart failure is being discharged with prescriptions for furosemide and lisinopril, a low-sodium diet handout, and daily weight instructions. When the nurse finishes explaining, the patient nods and says, 'Yes, I understand.' The patient has not asked any questions. What is the best nursing action before discharge?
options: Ask the patient to explain in their own words how they will take the medications and monitor their weight
Give the patient the written handouts and schedule a follow-up phone call for the next day
Ask the patient's daughter to listen to the instructions since she will be helping at home
Have the patient sign the discharge instructions to confirm they were received
rationale: Teach-back is the evidence-based method for confirming comprehension; nodding and saying 'I understand' does not verify learning, especially in patients who may be reluctant to admit confusion. Handouts and follow-up calls are adjuncts, not substitutes for real-time confirmation. Delegating to the daughter excludes the patient, and a signature only confirms receipt, not understanding.

stem: A 54-year-old patient is being discharged 48 hours after an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She lives alone, reads at a basic level, and tells the nurse, 'Just give me the papers; I'll read them at home.' Which discharge approach best meets her learning needs?
options: Provide the standard written packet and reinforce that she can call with questions
Prioritize verbal instruction with demonstration, limit written material to large-print essentials, and use teach-back
Delay discharge teaching until she agrees to read the full packet
Have her watch a 30-minute educational video and sign that she completed it
rationale: Patients with limited literacy learn better through plain-language verbal teaching, demonstration, and simplified large-print materials confirmed with teach-back. Relying on a written packet she admits she will not study is ineffective. Delaying discharge is unnecessary and impractical, and passive video viewing without confirmation does not verify comprehension.

stem: During admission, a nurse wants to screen a 72-year-old patient for limited health literacy before providing teaching about a new insulin regimen. Which question is the most appropriate single-item screening approach?
options: Ask, 'How confident are you filling out medical forms by yourself?'
Ask, 'What is the highest grade you completed in school?'
Ask, 'Do you have trouble reading the newspaper?'
Ask, 'Can you show me your medication list from home?'
rationale: 'How confident are you filling out medical forms by yourself?' is the validated single-item health literacy screener with the best sensitivity; it is nonjudgmental and functional. Years of schooling correlate poorly with health literacy, newspaper reading is stigmatizing and imprecise, and a home medication list does not screen literacy.

stem: A 45-year-old patient with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes tells the nurse, 'I already know all about diabetes — my whole family has it.' Her HbA1c is 11.2% and she has never checked her blood glucose. What is the best nursing response?
options: Accept her statement and move on to scheduling her follow-up appointment
Say, 'Since your family has it, you can probably skip the diabetes class'
Explore what she knows and believes about diabetes before planning teaching, using open-ended questions
Provide a comprehensive diabetes education packet so she has complete information
rationale: Assessing current knowledge, beliefs, and practices is the essential first step in patient education; her claim of knowledge conflicts with her uncontrolled disease, suggesting gaps or misconceptions. Accepting her statement or skipping teaching abandons the learning need. A packet alone ignores her motivation and health literacy level.

stem: A 60-year-old patient newly diagnosed with COPD is prescribed a tiotropium inhaler and a rescue albuterol inhaler. During teaching he repeatedly confuses which inhaler to use daily versus during flare-ups. What is the best nursing action?
options: Repeat the same verbal explanation a third time until he can recite the difference
Tell him to use whichever inhaler is closest when he feels short of breath
Label the inhalers with simple cues such as 'every day' and 'rescue/breathing trouble,' demonstrate each, and have him demonstrate back
Write out the full medication inserts for both inhalers and highlight the key sections
rationale: When verbal teaching fails, adding concrete cues, demonstration, and return demonstration addresses the learning gap; confusing maintenance and rescue inhalers is a common and dangerous error. Repeating the same failed method rarely works. Using whichever is closest risks overusing tiotropium, and full package inserts overwhelm rather than clarify.

stem: A 58-year-old patient is starting warfarin after a new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. She asks, 'Can I still take my ibuprofen for arthritis and eat my usual big spinach salads?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell her both are fine as long as she takes the warfarin at the same time each day
Advise her to avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen because of bleeding risk and to keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than eliminating spinach
Tell her to stop eating spinach completely and take ibuprofen only with food
Reassure her that warfarin has no significant food or drug interactions at her dose
rationale: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk with warfarin and should be avoided, while vitamin K intake should be kept consistent (not eliminated) to keep the INR stable. Eliminating spinach entirely is unnecessary and disrupts her diet; reassuring her there are no interactions is false and dangerous. Timing of the dose does not mitigate these interactions.

stem: A 52-year-old patient had a new colostomy created 3 days ago and refuses to look at or touch the stoma, saying, 'I can't deal with this — my wife will do it.' His wife appears anxious and overwhelmed. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Respect his refusal and teach the wife exclusively, since she volunteered
Acknowledge his feelings, normalize the adjustment, and begin with small steps such as observing and then touching the stoma, involving both patient and wife
Tell him that insurance requires him to learn self-care before discharge
Show him graphic photos of other patients' stomas to desensitize him quickly
rationale: Grief and altered body image are normal after ostomy surgery; acknowledging feelings and using gradual desensitization with the patient and caregiver builds self-efficacy. Teaching only the wife leaves the patient dependent and unprepared. Coercion through insurance claims is unethical, and graphic photos can increase distress.

stem: A 38-year-old patient with type 1 diabetes is being discharged with a new insulin pump. She demonstrates correct pump programming but cannot explain what to do if the pump alarms for an occlusion while she is at work. What should the nurse do?
options: Document that she passed the programming competency and discharge her
Advise her to ignore occlusion alarms for up to 4 hours since they are usually false
Tell her to remove the pump and go to the emergency department for any alarm
Provide written troubleshooting steps, have her practice the occlusion response with teach-back, and confirm she carries backup insulin and supplies
rationale: Safe pump use requires knowing alarm responses, not just programming; occlusion can rapidly lead to DKA in type 1 diabetes, so backup insulin and practiced troubleshooting are essential. Passing programming alone is an incomplete competency. ED visits for every alarm are impractical, and ignoring occlusion alarms is dangerous.

stem: A 29-year-old patient who is a visual learner needs teaching about wound care for a surgical incision. Which method best matches his learning style?
options: Give a detailed verbal explanation while he rests with his eyes closed
Provide step-by-step diagrams and a video demonstration, then have him perform the dressing change
Read the discharge instructions aloud slowly twice
Have him listen to an audio recording of the wound care instructions
rationale: Visual learners retain information best through diagrams, videos, and observed demonstration paired with hands-on return demonstration. Verbal-only or audio-only methods mismatch his style. Reading aloud slowly does not add a visual component and is less effective for psychomotor skills.

stem: A 76-year-old patient is being discharged after a hip fracture repair. She lives with her elderly husband, who has early dementia. The nurse has 20 minutes for discharge teaching. What is the priority?
options: Focus on the critical safety items — fall precautions, hip precautions, medication essentials, and warning signs — using teach-back, and arrange home health follow-up
Teach every detail of the medication list, diet, wound care, and follow-up in the available time
Give the couple the full written packet and tell them to call the surgeon with questions
Postpone teaching until the patient's adult children can be present
rationale: With limited time and a cognitively vulnerable caregiver dyad, prioritizing critical safety content confirmed by teach-back plus home health reinforcement is the safest approach. Trying to cover everything superficially guarantees nothing is learned. Relying on the packet alone is unsafe, and postponing teaching leaves them unprepared at discharge.

stem: A nurse is using teach-back with a patient learning to use a peak flow meter. The patient performs the steps incorrectly. What is the best nursing response?
options: Say, 'You did that wrong — let me show you again,' and repeat the demonstration
Re-explain using a different approach and say, 'I want to make sure I explained this clearly — can you show me again how you'll do it at home?'
Document that the patient failed teach-back and is not ready for discharge
Ask the patient why they are not paying attention
rationale: Effective teach-back frames the re-teaching as the nurse's responsibility ('I want to make sure I explained clearly'), which preserves dignity and encourages retry without shame. Blaming the patient or questioning their attention damages rapport and motivation. A single failed attempt does not mean the patient cannot learn; it signals the teaching method needs adjustment.

stem: A 63-year-old patient takes 11 prescription medications and tells the nurse, 'I take the white pill in the morning and the blue one at night — I can't pronounce the names.' His pill bottles show he is mixing up two similarly shaped tablets. What is the best nursing intervention?
options: Tell him he must learn the generic names of all his medications before discharge
Advise him to stop taking the medications he cannot identify until the pharmacist calls him
Create a personalized pill schedule with pictures, colors, times, and purposes, and reconcile it with teach-back
Suggest he ask his neighbor to sort his pills each week
rationale: A personalized visual medication schedule using pill appearance, timing, and purpose accommodates limited health literacy and directly addresses the mix-up; teach-back confirms safety. Demanding he learn generic names is unrealistic and shaming. Stopping unidentified medications risks harm, and delegating to a neighbor is unreliable and raises privacy concerns.

stem: A 41-year-old patient newly diagnosed with hypertension says, 'I feel fine, so I don't need medicine. I'll just cut back on coffee.' His blood pressure is 178/104 mm Hg. What is the best nursing response?
options: Agree that lifestyle changes alone are a reasonable first step given how he feels
Explain that hypertension is usually symptomless and that sustained pressures at his level can damage the heart, kidneys, and brain, then explore his concerns about medication
Tell him he will have a stroke if he does not start medication today
Document refusal and cancel the prescription
rationale: Addressing the 'I feel fine' misconception with factual risk information while exploring his concerns respects autonomy and targets the actual barrier to adherence. Agreeing with lifestyle-only management is unsafe at 178/104. Fear-based threats and documenting refusal without discussion abandon the teaching opportunity.

stem: A 33-year-old postpartum patient being discharged after a cesarean birth asks when she should call the provider. Which teaching point takes priority?
options: Call if lochia changes to bright red heavy bleeding soaking a pad hourly, or with fever, foul odor, or severe headache
Call if she feels tired during the first week at home
Call if the baby sleeps more than 3 hours at a stretch
Call if she has mild incisional itching as it heals
rationale: Heavy bright-red bleeding, fever, foul-smelling lochia, and severe headache are warning signs of hemorrhage, infection, or preeclampsia that require urgent evaluation. Fatigue, infant sleep patterns, and mild itching are expected or lower-acuity issues. Prioritizing red-flag symptoms is the core of safe discharge teaching.

stem: A 66-year-old patient is starting home CPAP for severe sleep apnea. At the first follow-up he reports using it 'a couple of hours' and removing the mask because it feels claustrophobic. His daytime sleepiness is unchanged. What is the best nursing action?
options: Tell him CPAP is not for everyone and suggest he stop using it
Document nonadherence and discontinue the CPAP order
Advise him to take a sedative each night so he sleeps through the discomfort
Assess mask fit and specific discomforts, suggest trying a different mask style, desensitization while awake, and ramp features, and reinforce benefits
rationale: Mask discomfort and claustrophobia are the most common and most fixable barriers to CPAP adherence; troubleshooting fit, style, and acclimation strategies directly addresses them. Abandoning therapy leaves severe apnea untreated. Sedatives worsen apnea, and documenting nonadherence without intervention misses the nursing role in adherence support.

stem: A 50-year-old patient scheduled for a colonoscopy asks the nurse, 'Do I really have to drink all of that prep? My friend said she just did an enema.' What is the best nursing response?
options: Say, 'Your friend's experience doesn't matter — just follow the orders'
Assess what the patient understands and fears about the bowel prep, then explain why complete prep is essential for polyp detection and what strategies ease it
Cancel the procedure since the patient is looking for shortcuts
Tell the patient the prep is optional if the stool looks clear
rationale: Assessing understanding and fears first allows targeted teaching about why adequate prep determines the exam's diagnostic value, plus practical coping strategies. Dismissing the concern shuts down dialogue. Canceling is an overreaction, and calling the prep optional is false and risks a nondiagnostic procedure.

stem: A nurse teaches a patient with low health literacy about taking apixaban. Which statement by the nurse best demonstrates the teach-back method?
options: 'I've given you a lot of information — to be sure I was clear, can you tell me how you'll take this blood thinner and what you'll watch for?'
'Do you understand how to take this medication?'
'Please repeat back word-for-word what I just told you'
'Your pharmacist will go over this again, so don't worry if you forget'
rationale: This phrasing places responsibility on the nurse's clarity, asks for explanation in the patient's own words, and covers both administration and monitoring — the hallmarks of proper teach-back. 'Do you understand?' invites a socially desirable yes. Word-for-word repetition tests memory, not comprehension. Deferring to the pharmacist abdicates the nurse's teaching role.

stem: A 70-year-old patient is prescribed alendronate for osteoporosis. She says she will take it with her morning coffee and then lie back down to rest. What is the priority teaching point?
options: Take it with a full glass of water, remain upright for 30 minutes, and take nothing else by mouth during that time
Take it at bedtime for better absorption
Take it with coffee since caffeine improves absorption
Lie flat after taking it to reduce dizziness
rationale: Alendronate must be taken with plain water on an empty stomach while remaining upright for at least 30 minutes to prevent esophageal irritation and ulceration; food, coffee, and other drugs impair absorption. Bedtime dosing and lying flat increase esophageal injury risk. Coffee does not improve absorption.

stem: A clinic nurse notices that several patients with diabetes repeatedly miss the link between their diet choices and blood glucose readings. Which system-level intervention best addresses health literacy?
options: Post the ADA Standards of Care on the waiting room wall
Implement plain-language, picture-based education materials and routine teach-back for all diabetes teaching
Require all patients to attend a 2-hour lecture before appointments
Mail patients their lab results with a note to look them up online
rationale: Universal plain-language materials with visual supports plus routine teach-back is the evidence-based, health-literate systems approach; it helps all patients regardless of literacy level. Posting clinical guidelines is written for professionals. Mandatory lectures ignore learning needs and access barriers, and mailing raw lab results without interpretation increases confusion.

stem: A 59-year-old patient is discharged after a transient ischemic attack with prescriptions for clopidogrel and atorvastatin. He asks, 'How will I know if this happens again?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell him TIAs never recur once medications are started
Tell him to take an extra clopidogrel if symptoms return
Teach BE-FAST warning signs, emphasize calling emergency services immediately rather than driving himself, and confirm with teach-back
Advise him to wait 24 hours to see if symptoms resolve before seeking care
rationale: BE-FAST education with explicit instruction to call emergency services addresses the critical time-sensitive response to recurrent TIA/stroke. TIAs frequently recur and herald stroke, so reassurance is false. Extra clopidogrel is not indicated, and waiting 24 hours wastes the treatment window.

stem: A 47-year-old patient is discharged with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) for 6 weeks of IV antibiotics. She lives alone and is anxious about managing it. What is the priority teaching focus?
options: Teach her to change the PICC dressing using sterile technique every day
Teach signs of infection and occlusion, activity and showering precautions, and when to call the home health nurse, with return demonstration of key steps
Give her the catheter manufacturer's 40-page manual to study
Tell her to avoid moving the arm at all for 6 weeks
rationale: For a patient with home health support, priority teaching is recognizing complications, protecting the line during activities of daily living, and knowing when to call — confirmed by return demonstration. Daily self dressing changes are typically done by the home nurse, not the patient. The full manual overwhelms, and total arm immobilization is unnecessary and harmful.

stem: A 36-year-old patient who describes herself as a kinesthetic learner needs to learn subcutaneous heparin injection technique before discharge. What is the best teaching method?
options: Provide a detailed written handout with diagrams
Explain the steps verbally in detail
Play an instructional video twice without practice
Have her practice the injection technique on a teaching pad and then on herself with coaching and return demonstration
rationale: Kinesthetic learners master psychomotor skills through hands-on practice; coached practice on a pad followed by supervised self-injection with return demonstration builds competence and confidence. Handouts, videos, and verbal explanations alone do not give her the tactile practice she needs for a self-injection skill.

stem: A nurse is discharging a patient with heart failure who must follow a 2-gram sodium diet. The patient correctly teaches back the diet when asked. Which additional action best reinforces long-term adherence?
options: Assume no further teaching is needed since teach-back was successful
Provide culturally tailored food examples and label-reading practice using foods the patient actually eats
Give a generic low-sodium diet pamphlet in English
Schedule teach-back again only if the patient is readmitted
rationale: Successful teach-back confirms initial understanding, but adherence depends on applying the diet to the patient's real foods and culture; label-reading practice with familiar foods bridges that gap. Assuming no further reinforcement is needed ignores the complexity of dietary change. Generic pamphlets and waiting for readmission are passive and ineffective.

stem: A 55-year-old patient newly diagnosed with atrial fibrillation is prescribed metoprolol. He asks, 'Will this fix my irregular heartbeat?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Explain that metoprolol controls heart rate and reduces symptoms but does not convert the rhythm, and teach pulse self-checks and when to seek care
Say, 'Yes, this will convert your heart back to normal rhythm'
Tell him the medication is only temporary and he can stop when he feels better
Advise him to double the dose if he feels palpitations
rationale: Accurate teaching distinguishes rate control from rhythm conversion, sets realistic expectations, and adds self-monitoring skills with clear action thresholds. Claiming it converts rhythm is false. Stopping when feeling better risks rebound effects, and doubling the dose for palpitations is unsafe.

stem: An 82-year-old patient with mild cognitive impairment is being discharged after pneumonia treatment. Her son, who works full-time, will check on her evenings. Which discharge plan best supports safe medication management?
options: Give her a 30-day pill organizer filled by the nurse and written instructions in small print
Simplify the regimen with the provider if possible, use a weekly pill organizer with large-print schedule, involve the son via teach-back, and arrange a home health or pharmacy follow-up
Tell her to keep all pill bottles on the kitchen counter so she remembers
Have the son quit his job to supervise medications
rationale: Cognitively impaired older adults need regimen simplification, visual organizers, caregiver involvement confirmed by teach-back, and professional follow-up — a layered safety approach. A nurse-filled organizer without follow-up or caregiver confirmation is a single fragile point of failure. Bottles on the counter invite errors, and asking the son to quit work is unrealistic.

stem: A 48-year-old patient consistently misses appointments, does not refill prescriptions on time, and nods politely during teaching but cannot describe his treatment plan. The nurse suspects limited health literacy. What is the best initial approach?
options: Confront him about nonadherence and document him as noncompliant
Order formal neuropsychological testing
Use the Newest Vital Sign or a similar validated brief screening tool in a nonjudgmental way and adopt universal health literacy precautions
Assume he is intentionally nonadherent and focus teaching on consequences
rationale: Brief validated screening plus universal precautions (plain language, teach-back, visual aids) addresses the likely root cause without stigma. Labeling him noncompliant or intentional ignores the literacy barrier and damages trust. Neuropsychological testing is disproportionate and does not assess health literacy.

stem: A 62-year-old patient starting insulin glargine at bedtime asks, 'What if my blood sugar drops in the middle of the night?' What is the priority teaching?
options: Reassure her that glargine never causes hypoglycemia
Teach the 15-15 rule, to keep fast-acting glucose at the bedside, recognize nocturnal hypoglycemia symptoms, and when to call for help
Tell her to skip the dose if she feels nervous about nighttime lows
Advise her to eat a large sugary snack every night before bed
rationale: All insulins carry hypoglycemia risk; teaching recognition, the 15-15 rule, bedside glucose availability, and escalation is the safety priority. Claiming glargine never causes lows is false. Skipping doses worsens control, and routine large sugary snacks undermine glycemic management.

stem: A 44-year-old patient with a new ileostomy is being taught to empty and change the pouching system. She performs the change correctly but says, 'I can never go out in public again — everyone will smell it.' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell her that odor is unavoidable and she should stay home for the first month
Validate her concern, teach odor-control strategies such as proper seal, pouch deodorants, and diet adjustments, and discuss gradual return to activities
Minimize her feelings by saying most people never notice
Change the subject to the mechanics of pouch changes
rationale: Validating the fear while teaching concrete odor-control strategies and planning graded return to activities addresses both the emotional and practical dimensions. Telling her to stay home reinforces isolation. Minimizing dismisses a legitimate concern, and changing the subject avoids it.

stem: Before teaching a 71-year-old patient about a new walker after hip surgery, the nurse learns the patient is hard of hearing, wears glasses, and is in moderate pain. What should the nurse do first?
options: Proceed with teaching immediately since discharge is in one hour
Give the walker manual to the roommate to explain later
Shout the instructions so the patient can hear
Address the barriers first: ensure hearing aids and glasses are in place, treat pain, reduce background noise, and face the patient when speaking
rationale: Sensory deficits and pain are modifiable barriers to learning; correcting them before teaching is a prerequisite for comprehension and safety with a new mobility device. Proceeding despite barriers wastes the teaching moment. Shouting distorts speech and feels disrespectful, and delegating to a roommate is inappropriate.

stem: A 39-year-old patient discharged after a deep vein thrombosis is prescribed rivaroxaban. She asks about alcohol use and upcoming dental surgery. What is the best nursing guidance?
options: Tell her moderate alcohol is safe and she can skip telling the dentist about the medication
Advise limiting alcohol due to bleeding risk and to inform all providers including the dentist, since procedures may require holding the dose per provider instructions
Tell her to stop rivaroxaban on her own 3 days before dental work
Reassure her that dental procedures have no bleeding risk on anticoagulants
rationale: Alcohol increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants, and invasive procedures require provider-directed perioperative planning — never self-directed holding. Skipping disclosure to the dentist is unsafe. Stopping on her own risks thrombosis, and claiming dental work has no bleeding risk is false.

stem: A nurse teaches a group of patients about low-sodium eating. One participant says, 'This is too much information — I can't remember all of this.' What is the best response using health literacy principles?
options: Chunk the information into small segments, focus on 2-3 key behaviors, and use teach-back after each segment
Continue with the full presentation since all the content is required
Hand out the slides and end the session early
Tell the participant to pay closer attention
rationale: Chunking content into small segments with teach-back after each respects cognitive load limits and is the core health-literate teaching strategy. Pushing through the full presentation guarantees poor retention. Ending early without confirming learning, or blaming the participant, abandons the teaching goal.

stem: A 57-year-old patient is discharged with a home blood pressure monitor. At follow-up, his log shows readings of 220/130, but he feels well and continued his routine. What is the priority nursing action?
options: Praise him for keeping a detailed log and continue current management
Assess his measurement technique and cuff size, verify the device's accuracy, and teach red-flag thresholds with clear action steps for severe readings
Tell him the monitor is broken and to throw it away
Advise him to stop checking his blood pressure since it causes anxiety
rationale: Extremely high readings in an asymptomatic patient most often reflect technique or equipment error, so validating technique, cuff fit, and device accuracy comes first — paired with teaching when to seek urgent care. Praising the log without questioning the values misses a safety issue. Discarding the monitor or stopping monitoring abandons needed surveillance.

stem: A 26-year-old patient with newly diagnosed epilepsy is prescribed levetiracetam twice daily. She works night shifts and says, 'I'll just take both pills when I wake up.' What is the best nursing intervention?
options: Agree that consolidated dosing is easier for shift workers
Tell her missing the exact 12-hour spacing will cause immediate brain damage
Explain why twice-daily spacing maintains seizure protection, help her anchor doses to her sleep-wake routine, and use teach-back
Document her plan and take no further action
rationale: Twice-daily antiepileptics need roughly even spacing for stable drug levels; anchoring doses to her actual routine (e.g., upon waking and before sleep) makes adherence feasible for shift work, confirmed by teach-back. Consolidating both doses risks toxicity then subtherapeutic levels. Fear-based warnings and passive documentation do not solve the adherence problem.

stem: A 64-year-old patient is discharged 2 days after a myocardial infarction with prescriptions for aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and atorvastatin. He asks, 'Which of these can I stop once I feel better?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell him he can stop the atorvastatin once his cholesterol improves

Explain that dual antiplatelet therapy and the other cardiac medications protect against another heart attack and stent clotting, must not be stopped without the cardiologist, and teach what to do if a dose is missed
Say he can stop any medication that causes side effects
Advise stopping clopidogrel first since it is the most expensive
rationale: Prematurely stopping dual antiplatelet therapy after MI/stent risks stent thrombosis and recurrent MI; teaching the protective purpose of each drug and the rule against unsupervised stopping is lifesaving. Stopping statins when 'better' or dropping the expensive drug invites catastrophe. Telling him to stop anything with side effects encourages unguided discontinuation instead of reporting.

stem: A 52-year-old patient who learns best by reading needs instruction on a new gluten-free diet for celiac disease. Which approach fits best?
options: Show a cooking demonstration video only
Have another patient explain the diet to her
Give a lengthy verbal lecture without handouts
Provide well-organized written materials with food lists and label-reading guides at an appropriate reading level, supplemented by brief discussion and teach-back
rationale: A reading-preference learner benefits most from organized written materials matched to her literacy level, with discussion and teach-back to confirm application. Video-only or lecture-only approaches mismatch her style, and peer teaching is unreliable for the strict accuracy celiac disease requires.

stem: A 49-year-old patient newly diagnosed with gout is prescribed allopurinol daily and colchicine for flares. He says, 'I'll just take the allopurinol when my toe hurts.' What is the priority teaching point?
options: Agree that as-needed dosing is acceptable for allopurinol
Explain that allopurinol is daily prevention that must be taken continuously even without symptoms, while colchicine is for acute flares, and warn that stopping allopurinol can trigger attacks
Tell him to double the allopurinol dose during a flare
Advise him to avoid all protein to prevent gout
rationale: Allopurinol lowers uric acid only with continuous daily use; taking it only during flares is ineffective and abrupt changes can precipitate attacks. Doubling the dose during flares is not indicated. Eliminating all protein is unnecessary and nutritionally harmful; the key distinction is daily prevention versus flare treatment.

stem: A nurse is teaching a patient's family caregiver to administer tube feedings. The caregiver correctly demonstrates the procedure. What is the best next step?
options: Ask the caregiver to teach back the signs of intolerance and aspiration and what to do if the tube dislodges
Document competency and end teaching
Assume the caregiver also understands the feeding schedule
Have the caregiver sign a waiver accepting responsibility
rationale: Psychomotor competency alone is incomplete; the caregiver must also teach back complication recognition and emergency responses, since aspiration and dislodgement are the highest-risk events. Assuming schedule understanding or ending teaching leaves critical gaps. A waiver does not ensure safety and shifts blame.

stem: A 61-year-old patient is discharged with a new prescription for potassium chloride after starting furosemide. He asks, 'Can't I just eat bananas instead?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell him bananas are equivalent and he can skip the prescription
Explain that food sources help but may not replace the prescribed supplement, teach signs of low potassium, and advise against doubling up or using salt substitutes without guidance
Tell him to take double the potassium dose and skip bananas
Advise him to stop the furosemide so he won't need potassium
rationale: Dietary potassium supports but does not reliably replace prescribed repletion in patients on loop diuretics; teaching hypokalemia signs and warning against salt substitutes (potassium chloride) prevents both deficiency and dangerous hyperkalemia from doubling up. Bananas alone are insufficient, and stopping furosemide abandons heart failure management.

stem: A 74-year-old patient with limited English proficiency needs teaching about wound care before discharge. His adult daughter interprets for the family. What is the best approach?
options: Teach in English slowly while the daughter interprets informally
Ask the daughter to translate the English handout at home later
Use a qualified medical interpreter, provide translated written materials at an appropriate literacy level, demonstrate the skill, and confirm with teach-back through the interpreter
Skip detailed teaching since the language barrier makes it ineffective
rationale: Qualified medical interpreters plus translated materials, demonstration, and interpreter-mediated teach-back is the standard for safe teaching across language barriers; family interpreters introduce errors and role conflicts. Having the daughter translate later is unreliable, and skipping teaching is unsafe.

stem: A 56-year-old patient is prescribed sertraline for depression and asks, 'How soon will I feel better? Can I stop it once I do?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell her she will feel better in 2 days and can stop then
Explain that improvement typically takes 4-6 weeks, the medication must be continued even after feeling better, and stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms
Advise doubling the dose if she doesn't feel better in one week
Tell her antidepressants are addictive so she should use the lowest dose for the shortest time
rationale: Setting realistic expectations about the 4-6 week onset, the need for continuation, and discontinuation syndrome directly addresses the two most common adherence failures with SSRIs. Promising 2-day relief is false. Doubling the dose is unsafe, and calling SSRIs addictive mischaracterizes them and discourages needed treatment.

stem: A 42-year-old patient admitted with cellulitis tells the nurse, 'Don't bother teaching me — I'm a nurse's aide and I already know this stuff.' The nurse notices she is elevating the infected leg below heart level. What is the best response?
options: Accept her background and skip teaching to respect her expertise
Lecture her on the correct elevation technique
Report her to her employer for poor practice
Gently note the observed practice, ask what she knows about elevation for cellulitis, and fill gaps collaboratively
rationale: Prior healthcare experience does not guarantee correct self-care knowledge; addressing the observed error through collaborative gap-filling respects her background while correcting the practice. Skipping teaching misses the demonstrated need. Reporting her is disproportionate, and lecturing damages rapport.

stem: A 67-year-old patient is discharged after a new pacemaker implant. Which instruction is the priority for the first 6 weeks?
options: Avoid lifting the arm on the pacemaker side above shoulder level and avoid heavy lifting to prevent lead dislodgement
Resume all normal activities including golf immediately to prevent stiffness
Sleep only on the pacemaker side to protect the device
Remove the pressure dressing at home on day 2
rationale: Restricting arm movement above shoulder level and heavy lifting for several weeks protects against lead dislodgement, the key early complication. Immediate full activity including golf risks dislodgement. Sleeping position does not protect the device, and dressing removal timing follows surgeon instructions, not patient preference.

stem: During discharge teaching, a patient correctly teaches back how to take a new medication but becomes tearful and says, 'There's just so much — I can't keep track of all these changes.' What is the best nursing response?
options: Continue with the remaining teaching points since they are all required
Pause, acknowledge feeling overwhelmed, prioritize the most critical safety information, use teach-back on those items, and arrange follow-up reinforcement
Tell the patient to calm down so teaching can continue
Document that the patient refused further teaching
rationale: Emotional overwhelm blocks learning; pausing to acknowledge feelings, prioritizing critical safety content, and planning follow-up reinforcement is the health-literate response. Pushing through guarantees poor retention. Telling the patient to calm down is dismissive, and documenting refusal mischaracterizes an overwhelmed learner.

stem: A 63-year-old patient with heart failure is discharged with a LifeVest wearable defibrillator while awaiting an ICD decision. He asks when he must wear it. What is the priority teaching point?
options: Wear it at all times except when showering, keep the battery charged, and ensure the monitor stays nearby
Wear it only when feeling palpitations
Wear it only at night while sleeping
Wear it only during exercise
rationale: The LifeVest only protects against sudden cardiac arrest while worn; continuous wear except brief showering with charged batteries is the lifesaving instruction. Wearing it only with symptoms, at night, or during exercise leaves lethal arrhythmias undetected most of the day.

stem: A nurse is creating a discharge instruction sheet for patients with low health literacy after total knee arthroplasty. Which design choice best supports comprehension?
options: Use 10-point font to fit all information on one page
Use plain language, large font, white space, pictures of exercises, and a checklist format
Include medical terminology so patients learn the correct terms
Print the sheet in light gray ink to look professional
rationale: Plain language, large readable font, white space, pictorial supports, and checklists are evidence-based health-literate design principles. Small font, dense text, jargon, and low-contrast ink all reduce comprehension, especially for older adults and low-literacy readers.

stem: A 37-year-old patient newly diagnosed with multiple sclerosis asks the nurse, 'Will I end up in a wheelchair?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Reassure her that most people with MS never have any disability
Tell her to expect wheelchair use within 5 years so she can plan
Provide honest, balanced information that the disease course varies widely, many people remain ambulatory, and focus teaching on symptom management and reliable information sources
Avoid the question and change the subject to medications
rationale: MS has a highly variable course; honest acknowledgment of uncertainty with balanced information and a pivot to actionable self-management respects her need to know without false reassurance or catastrophic prediction. Guaranteeing no disability is false, predicting wheelchair use is unsupported, and avoiding the question abandons her.

stem: A 58-year-old patient is discharged on enoxaparin injections after a DVT. She is afraid of needles and says her husband will give the injections. What is the best nursing action?
options: Insist she learn self-injection since it is her medication
Teach the husband the injection technique with return demonstration, teach both of them the signs of bleeding and when to call, and confirm with teach-back
Give her oral medication instead without a provider order
Tell her to skip doses on days her husband is unavailable
rationale: When a willing caregiver is available, training the caregiver with return demonstration plus teaching both partners bleeding precautions and escalation is safe and patient-centered. Forcing self-injection on a needle-phobic patient invites missed doses. Changing prescriptions requires a provider order, and skipping doses risks clot extension.

stem: A 64-year-old retired teacher who is an auditory learner needs teaching about a new low-sodium diet. Which method best fits her learning style?
options: Give her only a printed diet handout to read silently
Have her practice reading nutrition labels without discussion
Show a silent video demonstration
Use a conversational discussion with verbal explanations, encourage her to repeat key points aloud, and supplement with a brief written summary
rationale: Auditory learners retain through listening and speaking; discussion with verbal repetition leverages her strength, while a brief written summary supports later reference. Silent reading-only or video-only approaches mismatch her style. Label practice without discussion misses the auditory component.

stem: A nurse asks a patient to teach back wound care instructions, and the patient says, 'I already told you I understand — are you questioning my intelligence?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Apologize and skip teach-back to avoid offending the patient
Explain that teach-back is routine for every patient to make sure the nurse explained clearly, and reframe: 'I want to be sure I did a good job explaining'
Insist the patient complete teach-back or discharge will be delayed
Document the patient as uncooperative
rationale: Normalizing teach-back as universal routine and framing it as a check on the nurse's teaching defuses the perceived insult and preserves the safety check. Skipping it abandons comprehension verification. Coercion and labeling the patient uncooperative damage the therapeutic relationship.

stem: A 71-year-old patient is prescribed donepezil for early Alzheimer's disease. His wife asks what to expect. What is the best nursing teaching?
options: Tell her it will reverse his memory loss within weeks
Explain it may modestly slow symptom progression but does not cure or reverse the disease, give it at bedtime, and report significant GI upset, bradycardia, or vivid dreams
Advise stopping it if she notices no improvement in one week
Tell her to give it in the morning with grapefruit juice
rationale: Accurate expectations — modest slowing of decline, not cure — plus administration timing and key adverse effects (GI, bradycardia, vivid dreams) supports safe use and adherence. Promising reversal is false. One week is too soon to judge, and grapefruit juice is not indicated; bedtime dosing reduces GI upset.

stem: A 46-year-old patient is discharged after an appendectomy with instructions to advance diet as tolerated. He asks when he can return to his warehouse job lifting 50-pound boxes. What is the best nursing guidance?
options: Advise avoiding heavy lifting for about 4-6 weeks per surgeon guidance to prevent hernia, and to confirm specific restrictions at follow-up
Tell him he can lift normally as soon as the pain stops
Tell him to return to full duty in 3 days to avoid deconditioning
Advise permanent lifting restrictions
rationale: Heavy lifting too soon after abdominal surgery risks incisional hernia; 4-6 weeks of restriction with surgeon confirmation is the standard guidance. Lifting when pain stops is too vague and risky. Three days is unsafe, and permanent restriction is unnecessary for uncomplicated recovery.

stem: A nurse wants to quickly estimate a patient's ability to understand prescription labels during a busy admission. Which brief tool is most appropriate?
options: Ask the patient to read a full paragraph from a consent form aloud
Use the Newest Vital Sign, which asks 6 questions about an ice cream nutrition label
Administer a 50-question reading comprehension exam
Ask the patient to spell 'medication' backwards
rationale: The Newest Vital Sign is a validated 3-minute health literacy screening tool using a nutrition label to assess prose, numeracy, and document literacy. Reading a consent paragraph aloud tests pronunciation, not comprehension. A 50-question exam is impractical, and spelling backwards tests attention, not health literacy.

stem: A 60-year-old patient newly diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed methotrexate weekly. She says, 'I'll take it every day like my other pills.' What is the priority nursing intervention?
options: Agree that daily dosing will work faster
Tell her to take it whenever she remembers
Urgently correct the misconception: methotrexate is taken ONCE weekly on the same day, daily dosing can cause fatal toxicity; use teach-back and consider a calendar aid
Suggest she skip weeks when her joints feel good
rationale: Daily methotrexate instead of weekly is a well-documented fatal medication error; urgent correction with teach-back and memory aids is a critical safety intervention. Agreeing with daily dosing could kill her. Taking it whenever remembered undermines efficacy, and skipping weeks allows disease progression.

stem: A 55-year-old patient with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes is motivated to learn but says, 'I work two jobs — I don't have time for classes.' What is the best nursing approach?
options: Insist he attend the full diabetes education series regardless of his schedule
Assess his specific knowledge gaps and deliver brief, prioritized teaching in short sessions matched to his availability, with written reinforcement
Tell him to quit one job to make time for his health
Provide no teaching since he cannot attend classes
rationale: Assessing gaps and delivering prioritized teaching in brief flexible sessions respects his motivation while working within real constraints; written reinforcement extends learning. Insisting on full classes ignores his reality and guarantees nonattendance. Telling him to quit a job is inappropriate, and providing nothing abandons him.

stem: A 73-year-old patient is discharged on multiple new cardiac medications after a stent placement. The nurse clusters all teaching into the last 10 minutes before discharge. What is the main problem with this approach?
options: The patient will remember the last items best, so this is actually ideal
Family members can learn it all in 10 minutes
Written materials make timing irrelevant
Cognitive overload at a stressful moment impairs retention; teaching should be spaced throughout the stay with teach-back
rationale: Massed last-minute teaching during the stress of discharge causes cognitive overload and poor retention; spaced teaching with teach-back throughout the stay is the evidence-based approach. Recency does not overcome overload. Written materials do not compensate for absent comprehension checks, and families face the same overload.

stem: A patient with heart failure teaches back fluid restriction correctly but cannot teach back daily weight monitoring. What should the nurse do?
options: Document successful teach-back since the majority was correct
Re-teach only the weight monitoring portion using a different strategy, then re-check with teach-back
Repeat the entire teaching session from the beginning
Discharge the patient since fluid restriction is the more important topic
rationale: Teach-back is item-specific; the failed component needs targeted re-teaching with a new approach and re-verification, not repetition of already-learned material. Documenting partial success as complete is inaccurate. Daily weights are a critical early warning for decompensation and cannot be skipped.

stem: A 59-year-old patient is prescribed a home nebulizer for COPD exacerbations. She has never used one. What is the essential teaching sequence?
options: Demonstrate assembly, medication measurement, breathing technique, and cleaning, then have her perform return demonstration with teach-back on when to use it versus the rescue inhaler
Hand her the device and instruction manual at discharge
Tell her to use the nebulizer for all breathing problems including colds
Advise sharing the nebulizer with her husband who also wheezes
rationale: Nebulizer competence requires demonstration plus return demonstration covering assembly, dosing, technique, cleaning, and appropriate use indications. A manual alone does not build skill. Using it for all breathing problems is inappropriate, and sharing equipment risks infection.

stem: A 40-year-old patient with asthma consistently uses her fluticasone inhaler only when wheezing. She says, 'Why use it when I feel fine?' What is the best nursing response?
options: Agree that as-needed use is logical
Explain the difference between daily controller and rescue medications using a simple analogy, demonstrate technique, and confirm with teach-back
Tell her she will end up hospitalized if she doesn't comply
Switch her to oral steroids without a provider order
rationale: The controller-versus-rescue distinction is the core asthma self-management concept; a plain-language analogy plus technique check and teach-back targets her exact misunderstanding. Agreeing with as-needed controller use undermines prevention. Threats damage rapport, and changing prescriptions requires a provider.

stem: A 65-year-old patient starting sotalol for atrial fibrillation asks about side effects to watch for. What is the priority teaching?
options: Tell her there are no significant side effects
Advise her to check her blood sugar more often
Teach to monitor for dizziness, unusually slow pulse, shortness of breath, and to report fainting, since sotalol can cause bradycardia and proarrhythmia
Tell her to avoid drinking water with the pill
rationale: Sotalol's key risks are bradycardia, hypotension, and proarrhythmia (including torsades); teaching pulse and symptom monitoring with clear report thresholds is the safety priority. Claiming no side effects is false and dangerous. Blood sugar monitoring is irrelevant, and water restriction is not indicated.

stem: A 51-year-old patient is discharged after a partial colectomy with a new ileostomy and a prescription for loperamide. She asks about diet. What is the best initial dietary guidance?
options: Resume a high-fiber diet immediately to normalize output
Start with low-residue foods, chew thoroughly, eat small frequent meals, and introduce new foods one at a time while monitoring output
Avoid all fluids to thicken the output
Eat only meat for the first month
rationale: A new ileostomy needs gradual diet advancement with low-residue foods, thorough chewing, and small frequent meals to prevent blockage while output stabilizes. Immediate high-fiber intake risks obstruction. Fluid restriction causes dehydration with an ileostomy, and a meat-only diet is nutritionally inadequate.

stem: A 68-year-old patient with newly diagnosed Parkinson's disease tells the nurse, 'My neighbor says this medicine causes gambling problems.' He is prescribed pramipexole. What is the best nursing response?
options: Dismiss the neighbor's comment as gossip
Assure him this side effect never happens
Tell him to stop the medication immediately
Acknowledge the concern, explain that dopamine agonists can cause impulse-control disorders in some patients, teach what to watch for, and encourage reporting changes to the provider
rationale: Impulse-control disorders are a real, documented risk of dopamine agonists; validating the concern and teaching specific warning signs empowers the patient and family to detect it early. Dismissing or denying the risk destroys trust if symptoms appear. Stopping abruptly without provider guidance risks withdrawal and symptom rebound.

stem: A nurse is teaching an older adult with hearing loss about a new medication regimen. Which teach-back adaptation is best?
options: Write the teach-back questions on a whiteboard in large print and have the patient write or point to responses
Speak louder and faster to get through the material
Skip teach-back since hearing loss makes it unreliable
Have the patient teach back to another patient in the room
rationale: Written large-print teach-back with pointing or writing bypasses the hearing barrier while preserving the comprehension check. Speaking louder and faster reduces clarity. Skipping teach-back abandons safety verification, and involving another patient violates privacy.

stem: A 35-year-old patient with limited health literacy is prescribed a complex tapering course of prednisone. The pharmacy label reads 'take as directed.' What is the best nursing action?
options: Tell her to follow the label exactly
Create a clear day-by-day calendar showing the exact number of tablets each day, review it with teach-back, and suggest a phone alarm
Tell her to take the same dose every day for simplicity
Advise her to stop the prednisone when she feels better
rationale: 'Take as directed' is meaningless without explicit directions; a visual day-by-day taper calendar with teach-back and reminders prevents the common errors of wrong-dose continuation or abrupt stopping. Taking a constant dose defeats the taper, and stopping early risks adrenal crisis and disease flare.

stem: A 44-year-old patient is discharged after treatment for a kidney stone with a ureteral stent in place. Which symptom requires urgent follow-up teaching emphasis?
options: Fever, chills, inability to urinate, or severe flank pain
Mild pink-tinged urine for a day or two
Mild urgency when urinating
Needing to urinate more often than usual
rationale: Fever, chills, anuria, or severe flank pain with a ureteral stent suggest infection or obstruction — urologic emergencies. Pink urine, urgency, and frequency are expected stent irritative symptoms. Teaching must distinguish expected effects from red flags.

stem: A 58-year-old patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes says, 'My uncle lost his leg to diabetes, and now it's my turn.' What is the best nursing response?
options: Tell him amputation is inevitable with diabetes
Explore his fears, explain that complications are not inevitable and that glucose control, foot care, and regular monitoring greatly reduce risk, then teach daily foot inspection
Minimize his concern by saying his uncle was an unusual case
Focus only on diet teaching and ignore the emotional statement
rationale: Fatalistic beliefs undermine self-management; exploring the fear and countering it with evidence that complications are largely preventable, paired with concrete foot-care teaching, addresses both emotion and behavior. Calling amputation inevitable reinforces hopelessness. Minimizing or ignoring the statement misses the motivational barrier.

stem: A 47-year-old patient who is a read/write learner is learning to manage a new colostomy. Which resource best supports his learning style?
options: A detailed step-by-step printed guide with checklists that he can annotate
An audio-only podcast about ostomy life
A single verbal demonstration with no written backup
A support group meeting with no written materials
rationale: Read/write learners process best through text they can study and annotate; a detailed printable guide with checklists matches his style and serves as home reference. Audio-only or verbal-only approaches mismatch his preference, and while support groups help emotionally, they do not provide the structured written instruction he needs.

stem: A nurse teaches a patient about signs of wound infection before discharge. The patient teaches back redness, swelling, and pain but omits fever and drainage. What is the best response?
options: Accept the teach-back as adequate since the main signs were named
Scold the patient for not listening carefully
Gently add the missing signs: 'You're right about those — also watch for fever and any drainage or bad smell. Can you tell me all the signs you'll watch for?'
Restart the entire discharge teaching from the beginning
rationale: Partial teach-back requires targeted completion: affirming what was correct, adding the missing elements, and re-checking the full set ensures complete understanding without shaming. Accepting incomplete recall leaves gaps in safety knowledge. Scolding or restarting everything is inefficient and damages rapport.

stem: A 69-year-old patient is prescribed tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia. He asks when to take it. What is the priority teaching point?
options: Take it in the morning on an empty stomach
Take it 30 minutes after the same meal each day, and rise slowly due to orthostatic hypotension risk
Take it only when urinary symptoms are bothersome
Take a double dose if he misses one
rationale: Tamsulosin should be taken 30 minutes after the same meal daily for consistent absorption, and first-dose orthostatic hypotension requires teaching to rise slowly — especially critical in older adults at fall risk. Morning empty-stomach dosing is incorrect. As-needed use is ineffective, and doubling after a missed dose is unsafe.

stem: A 62-year-old patient is discharged after a COPD exacerbation with a new prescription for prednisone taper and home oxygen at 2 L/min. He is a current smoker. What is the priority safety teaching?
options: Teach that smoking near oxygen is a severe fire hazard and smoking must stop around oxygen; offer cessation resources
Tell him to increase oxygen to 4 L if he feels short of breath
Advise removing the oxygen when smoking to be safe
Focus only on the prednisone taper and skip smoking discussion
rationale: Oxygen plus smoking is a fire and explosion hazard and continued smoking undermines COPD treatment; addressing it head-on with cessation support is the safety priority. Increasing oxygen without orders is unsafe. Removing oxygen to smoke defeats therapy, and skipping the discussion ignores a lethal risk.

stem: A 57-year-old patient with heart failure is confused by the instruction 'limit fluids to 2 liters per day.' What is the best nursing approach?
options: Repeat '2 liters per day' firmly until she remembers
Give her a metric conversion chart to memorize
Tell her to just drink when thirsty and not worry about measuring
Convert the restriction into concrete terms using her own cups and containers, demonstrate measuring, and confirm with teach-back
rationale: Abstract measurements become actionable when translated into the patient's own household containers with demonstration and teach-back. Repeating the same abstract instruction does not build understanding. Drinking to thirst ignores the restriction, and a conversion chart adds cognitive burden without practical meaning.

stem: A 66-year-old patient is discharged after new-onset atrial fibrillation with a prescription for diltiazem. She drinks 4 cups of coffee daily and takes an over-the-counter decongestant for allergies. What is the priority teaching?
options: Explain that excessive caffeine and decongestants containing pseudoephedrine can trigger rapid heart rates and should be limited or avoided, and teach pulse monitoring
Tell her coffee and decongestants have no effect on heart rhythm
Advise doubling the diltiazem on days she drinks extra coffee
Tell her to stop the diltiazem if her pulse feels normal
rationale: Stimulants like caffeine and pseudoephedrine can precipitate tachyarrhythmias and counteract rate control; teaching avoidance plus self pulse-monitoring addresses a modifiable trigger. Claiming no effect is false. Doubling diltiazem is unsafe, and stopping when feeling normal invites rebound tachycardia.

stem: A 43-year-old patient newly diagnosed with hypothyroidism is prescribed levothyroxine. She takes a multivitamin with iron and calcium at breakfast with coffee. What is the priority teaching?
options: Take levothyroxine with the multivitamin for convenience
Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast, separating it from iron, calcium, and coffee
Take levothyroxine at bedtime with a calcium-rich snack
Double the dose on days she feels tired
rationale: Levothyroxine absorption is markedly reduced by food, coffee, iron, and calcium; empty-stomach dosing with separation is essential for stable thyroid levels. Taking it with the multivitamin impairs absorption. Bedtime dosing with calcium is incorrect, and doubling for fatigue is unsafe.

stem: A nurse is teaching a young adult with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes about hypoglycemia management. The patient teaches back the 15-15 rule perfectly but rolls their eyes and says, 'Yeah, yeah, I got it.' What is the best nursing response?
options: Accept the teach-back and move on since it was technically correct
Acknowledge the attitude without judgment, explore barriers such as diabetes distress or denial, and connect hypoglycemia planning to the patient's own goals
Lecture the patient about the dangers of a dismissive attitude
Document the patient as noncompliant with teaching
rationale: Technically correct teach-back paired with dismissive affect signals possible diabetes distress or denial; exploring barriers and linking safety planning to personal goals addresses the real obstacle to self-management. Accepting it at face value ignores the warning sign. Lecturing or labeling noncompliant damages the relationship.

stem: A 78-year-old patient with macular degeneration needs to learn a new eye-drop regimen for glaucoma. What is the best teaching adaptation?
options: Provide standard small-print written instructions
Use large-print, high-contrast step-by-step instructions, tactile markers on bottles, demonstration with return demonstration, and involve a family member with teach-back
Tell her to have the pharmacy put all drops in one bottle
Advise her to guess the timing since exact schedules don't matter
rationale: Vision loss demands large-print high-contrast materials, tactile cues, hands-on return demonstration, and caregiver backup confirmed by teach-back. Standard small print is unreadable for her. Combining drops in one bottle is unsafe and impractical, and timing does matter for intraocular pressure control.

stem: A 60-year-old patient scheduled for elective knee replacement says, 'I don't want to know the details — just do what you need to do.' Surgery is in 3 days. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Respect his coping style, provide only the essential safety information he must know, and offer to share more whenever he is ready
Force a full detailed explanation of the procedure since informed consent requires it
Cancel the surgery until he agrees to complete teaching
Give him a detailed surgical textbook to read
rationale: Patients have different information-seeking coping styles; respecting an avoidant style while ensuring essential safety knowledge and leaving the door open balances autonomy with safety. Forcing detail increases distress without improving outcomes. Canceling surgery is disproportionate, and a textbook overwhelms.

stem: A 55-year-old patient is discharged after a pulmonary embolism with instructions to wear compression stockings. She asks how long to wear them each day. What is the best nursing guidance?
options: Wear them during the day, remove at night, ensure proper fit without wrinkles or rolling, and inspect skin daily
Wear them only at night while sleeping
Wear them continuously for a month without removal
Wear them only when her legs hurt
rationale: Compression stockings are worn during waking hours to aid venous return and removed at night, with attention to fit and skin inspection to prevent skin breakdown. Night-only wear misses the therapeutic window. Continuous month-long wear risks skin injury, and as-needed wear is ineffective for prevention.

stem: A 71-year-old patient is discharged with a walker after a total hip replacement using a posterior approach. Which teaching point is the priority?
options: Teach her to bend at the waist to pick up objects from the floor
Teach hip precautions: no bending past 90 degrees, no crossing legs, no internal rotation, and use of adaptive equipment, confirmed with return demonstration
Tell her the walker is optional once she feels steady
Advise sitting in low soft chairs for comfort
rationale: Posterior hip precautions prevent prosthesis dislocation, the major early complication; teaching them with adaptive equipment and return demonstration is the safety priority. Bending to the floor violates precautions. The walker is essential initially, and low soft chairs force hip flexion past 90 degrees.

stem: A nurse uses teach-back with a patient learning to check blood glucose. The patient performs the fingerstick correctly but cannot state what the numbers mean. What is the best action?
options: Document successful teach-back since the skill was performed
Teach the target range and what high and low readings mean for action, using the patient's own recent readings, and re-check with teach-back
Tell the patient the numbers don't matter as long as the technique is right
Have the patient write down every reading to show the provider later
rationale: Technique without interpretation is incomplete self-monitoring; teaching target ranges and action thresholds using the patient's own numbers makes the data meaningful and actionable. Documenting partial success is inaccurate. Claiming numbers don't matter defeats the purpose of monitoring, and merely logging without understanding delays action.

stem: A 52-year-old patient with low health literacy is starting a complex HIV antiretroviral regimen. Which adherence strategy is best?
options: Give her the full medication guide to read at home
Simplify with a picture-based pill organizer system, link doses to daily routines, use teach-back, and arrange close follow-up
Tell her adherence matters but leave the planning to her
Advise taking all pills at random times to fit her schedule
rationale: Antiretroviral effectiveness depends on near-perfect adherence; visual organizers, routine-linking, teach-back, and close follow-up provide the structured support low-literacy patients need. A dense medication guide overwhelms. Leaving planning to her or endorsing random timing invites resistance and treatment failure.

stem: A 64-year-old patient newly diagnosed with chronic kidney disease stage 3 asks what he can do to protect his kidneys. What is the priority teaching?
options: Tell him nothing can slow kidney disease so he should not worry
Teach blood pressure and diabetes control, avoiding NSAIDs and nephrotoxins, limiting sodium, and keeping follow-up labs
Advise a high-protein diet to strengthen the kidneys
Tell him to drink 5 liters of water daily to flush the kidneys
rationale: CKD progression is slowed by controlling blood pressure and glucose, avoiding nephrotoxins like NSAIDs, moderating sodium and protein, and monitoring labs — actionable self-management. Claiming nothing helps is false and hopeless. High protein and excessive water intake can worsen CKD.

stem: A 48-year-old patient is discharged with a Jackson-Pratt drain after mastectomy. She is anxious about managing it at home. What is the priority teaching?
options: Tell her the drain will manage itself and she just needs to wait
Teach how to empty, measure, and record output, maintain suction by compressing the bulb, secure the drain, recognize infection signs, and know the removal criteria
Advise her to remove the drain herself when output looks low
Tell her to keep the drain clamped shut at all times
rationale: Safe JP drain management requires teaching emptying, measuring, recording, maintaining suction, securing, infection recognition, and follow-up criteria. Drains do not manage themselves. Self-removal risks injury and infection, and keeping it clamped defeats suction drainage.

stem: A 30-year-old patient who learns best through discussion and questioning needs teaching about a new diagnosis of ulcerative colitis. What is the best approach?
options: Hand her a pamphlet and leave the room
Use an interactive dialogue: explain key concepts, invite questions, use the ask-tell-ask technique, and confirm understanding with teach-back
Play a recorded lecture with no interaction
Have her read the medical textbook chapter silently
rationale: Discussion-oriented learners need interactive dialogue; ask-tell-ask invites their questions, corrects misconceptions, and builds on their engagement, with teach-back confirming learning. A pamphlet without dialogue, passive recordings, and silent textbook reading all mismatch her style and miss the chance to address fears about a chronic disease.

stem: A nurse is discharging a patient with limited English proficiency through an interpreter. The patient teaches back medication instructions correctly. What should the nurse do next?
options: Assume all other discharge topics are understood
Use teach-back through the interpreter for each critical topic: warning signs, follow-up, and diet
End teaching since the interpreter's time is limited
Have the patient sign the English discharge papers as confirmation
rationale: Teach-back must cover each critical domain, not just medications; interpreter-mediated teach-back for warning signs, follow-up, and diet ensures comprehensive safe discharge. Assuming global understanding from one topic is unsafe. Rushing due to interpreter time or relying on a signature in an unreadable language abandons verification.

stem: A 59-year-old patient is prescribed gabapentin for neuropathic pain, titrated gradually. He says, 'I'll start with the full dose to get faster relief.' What is the priority teaching?
options: Agree that faster titration gives faster relief
Explain that gabapentin must be titrated slowly to reduce dizziness and sedation, sudden full dosing increases fall and side-effect risk, and the drug takes time to reach full effect
Tell him gabapentin works immediately like an opioid
Advise stopping it abruptly if he feels dizzy
rationale: Gradual titration minimizes sedation, dizziness, and fall risk — especially important in older adults — and the full analgesic effect takes time; this directly counters his plan. Agreeing with full-dose initiation is unsafe. Gabapentin is not immediate like opioids, and abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms.

stem: A 45-year-old patient with diabetes cannot interpret the sliding-scale insulin instructions written as 'take X units per Y mg/dL range.' What is the best nursing intervention?
options: Tell her to estimate the dose based on how she feels
Advise her to take the same dose every time regardless of reading
Rewrite the scale as a simple table matching her meter's readings to exact doses, color-code ranges, practice with sample readings, and confirm with teach-back
Tell her to skip insulin when the instructions confuse her
rationale: Translating the sliding scale into a personalized, color-coded lookup table with practice and teach-back makes complex numeracy demands manageable and prevents dangerous dosing errors. Estimating by feel, fixed dosing, or skipping doses all risk severe hypo- or hyperglycemia.

stem: A 70-year-old patient is discharged after a transient ischemic attack. His wife asks what lifestyle changes matter most. What is the priority teaching?
options: Focus only on reducing stress through meditation
Teach the highest-impact changes: smoking cessation, blood pressure control, statin adherence, regular activity, and a heart-healthy diet, prioritized to what the couple can tackle first
Tell them lifestyle changes don't matter after a TIA
Advise a complete dietary overhaul starting tomorrow with no support
rationale: Secondary stroke prevention rests on evidence-based targets — smoking cessation, BP control, statins, activity, diet — prioritized realistically rather than overwhelming the couple. Meditation alone is insufficient. Claiming lifestyle doesn't matter is false, and demanding an unsupported overnight overhaul invites failure.

stem: A 38-year-old patient with newly diagnosed hypertension says, 'I read online that blood pressure medicine causes cancer, so I won't take it.' What is the best nursing response?
options: Dismiss the internet as unreliable and tell him to follow orders
Explore what he read and his specific fears, provide evidence-based information about his prescribed medication's safety profile, and discuss his values and options
Agree that the risk is real and he should avoid medication
Document refusal and end the conversation
rationale: Misinformation-driven refusal requires exploring the specific belief, providing accurate evidence about the actual drug, and engaging in shared decision-making — not dismissal or agreement with falsehoods. Dismissing him shuts down dialogue. Agreeing with the false claim is dishonest, and documenting refusal without discussion abandons him.

stem: A nurse teaches a caregiver to perform sterile dressing changes. The caregiver's teach-back is correct. Which statement best reinforces long-term success?
options: 'You did that perfectly — you won't have any problems at home'
'You demonstrated the steps well. Let's also review what you'll do if the dressing gets wet or you notice increased drainage, and here's the number to call with questions'
'Now you know more than most nurses'
'Try not to think about doing it wrong'
rationale: Affirming correct performance while adding contingency planning for common problems and a contact number prepares the caregiver for real-world variation. Promising no problems is false reassurance. Flattery is unprofessional, and telling them not to think about errors increases anxiety without adding skill.

stem: A 62-year-old patient is prescribed a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) unit for chronic back pain. What is the essential safety teaching?
options: Tell him to use it continuously 24 hours a day
Teach proper electrode placement, starting at low intensity, avoiding use over the chest, eyes, or broken skin, and not to use it while driving or sleeping
Advise placing electrodes directly over the spine at maximum intensity
Tell him the TENS unit will cure the underlying back problem
rationale: TENS safety requires correct pad placement, gradual intensity, and avoiding high-risk areas (chest, eyes, broken skin) and hazardous situations (driving, sleeping). Continuous 24-hour use risks skin injury. Maximum intensity over the spine is unsafe, and TENS manages symptoms rather than curing pathology.

stem: A 69-year-old patient with heart failure weighs himself daily but does not know what weight gain should prompt a call. His log shows a 4-pound gain over 2 days. What is the best nursing action?
options: Reassure him that 4 pounds is normal fluctuation
Teach the specific action threshold — call for a 2-3 pound gain in 24 hours or 5 pounds in a week — write it on his log, and confirm with teach-back
Tell him to stop weighing himself since it causes worry
Advise him to double his diuretic on his own
rationale: Daily weights are useless without an action threshold; teaching the 2-3 lb/24 hr or 5 lb/week rule, written directly on his log with teach-back, converts monitoring into early intervention. Calling 4 pounds in 2 days normal misses decompensation. Stopping monitoring or self-adjusting diuretics are both unsafe.

stem: A 53-year-old patient is discharged after a new diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis. He is a long-haul truck driver. What is the priority occupational teaching?
options: Tell him he can never drive again
Teach strategies for his job: frequent stops to walk and stretch, staying hydrated, wearing compression stockings, and continuing anticoagulation without missing doses on the road
Advise him to sit as still as possible during long hauls to avoid dislodging the clot
Tell him anticoagulation is only needed for one week
rationale: Prolonged immobility is his major modifiable risk; teaching movement breaks, hydration, compression, and uninterrupted anticoagulation directly addresses his occupational hazard. Permanent driving prohibition is unnecessary. Sitting still increases risk, and one week of anticoagulation is inadequate for DVT.

stem: A 50-year-old patient newly diagnosed with sleep apnea is prescribed CPAP but says, 'I don't snore that loud — this can't be serious.' His study showed an AHI of 42. What is the best nursing response?
options: Agree that mild snoring doesn't require treatment
Explain that severe apnea stresses the heart and brain even without loud snoring, link treatment to his reported daytime fatigue and hypertension, and address his specific concerns about CPAP
Tell him he will die in his sleep without CPAP
Order the CPAP without further discussion
rationale: An AHI of 42 is severe; explaining the cardiovascular and cognitive risks, connecting treatment to his own symptoms, and addressing CPAP concerns targets his minimization directly. Agreeing treatment is unnecessary is false and dangerous. Death threats are coercive, and ordering without discussion ignores autonomy.

stem: During a busy shift, a nurse is tempted to skip teach-back for a patient starting a new anticoagulant. Which rationale best supports taking the time?
options: Teach-back is required only for research studies
Patients prefer teach-back to all other methods
Teach-back takes less time than handing out pamphlets
Teach-back is the standard for confirming understanding of high-risk medications, and misunderstanding anticoagulants can cause fatal bleeding or clotting
rationale: Anticoagulants are high-risk drugs where misunderstanding causes hemorrhage or thrombosis; teach-back is the evidence-based standard for verifying comprehension of such critical teaching. It is standard practice, not research-only. Time comparisons and patient preferences are secondary to the safety imperative.

stem: A 44-year-old patient with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes is eager to learn but becomes confused when the nurse uses the terms 'glycemic index' and 'postprandial.' What should the nurse do?
options: Continue using the terms so the patient learns medical vocabulary
Switch to plain language, check understanding frequently, and define any necessary terms in simple words
Give the patient a medical dictionary
Assume the patient cannot learn diabetes management
